about: Blind re-grade of two eval runs of 2026-10-03, to decide whether to remove the regex filter for uncited 'the handbook doesn't say' sentences. 'cut' is branch simplify-gaps without that filter, measured before the rule dropping uncited sentences about 'the passages' was added; 'baseline' is the same eval run on answer-improvements at d10ccec, with the filter. The runs were anonymized; two graders per run, separate Claude agents that saw the questions and reference answers, the answers as shown (with the uncited text the app shows grey), and the parsed handbook, but not which run was which, the README or earlier grades, graded every row. They rated both runs the same: 21/30 correct and 2 false-absence each, on different questions. The cut run had more answers with a remark about the passages (7 vs 5), and both of its false-absence answers came from an uncited sentence starting 'The passages don't ...'. The 'passages' rule was added because of that: run offline over the cut's saved answers through the gate, it drops 8 sentences in 7 answers, including those two, and leaves the gaps shown. Per row, grade, metaRemark and note are grader 1's; grader2 and metaRemark2 are grader 2's.

grades.correct: answers what was asked, consistent with the reference answer and the handbook
grades.partially-correct: right, but misses a material part of what was asked, or hedges where the handbook is clear
grades.false-absence: says or implies that the handbook (or the passages) doesn't say something it does say
grades.missed-gap-named: doesn't give the asked-for information, but lists it as not found instead of denying it (a safe miss)
grades.declined-answerable: said not found, though the handbook answers it (a safe failure)
grades.declined-correctly: out of scope, and said not found
grades.oos-partial-gap-named: out of scope; answered only with cited facts, and named what is missing
grades.incorrect: answers a different question than the one asked, or states something the handbook contradicts
grades.oos-misleading: out of scope; the partial answer misleads (irrelevant facts presented as the answer, or invents the missing detail)

A few hours a month on a paid side gig is acceptable, provided it's done in your personal time and doesn't impact your work at PostHog.[1]

- The handbook says PostHog is ok with you earning money on the side, but not with it being your main focus and PostHog being just a paycheck.[2]
- Check in with the relevant Exec team member for your team (James, Tim, or Charles) to get their confirmation before going ahead with any side gig.[3] If the side gig existed before you joined, this will usually be covered during onboarding.[4]
- If an idea or project comes out of your work at PostHog, it should be treated as PostHog work by default.[5] To develop it as an external project, get explicit sign-off first.[6]
- If you may want the side gig to become your full-time work one day, let PostHog know so they can create a plan.[7]
rows.note: Matches p965 (a few hours a month, personal time, no impact on work); extra points on Exec sign-off and IP all supported by p965-966.

No. The handbook says PostHog doesn't contract deliverables, and especially doesn't contract to provide deliverables by a certain date, because on principle a single customer would then be forcing PostHog to build something.[1]

Some related points from the handbook:
- PostHog is willing to walk away from a deal if it would have to compromise on these principles, and it can do this because it has a strong growth engine with its ICP customers.[2]
- PostHog will build things for a big customer as long as it is confident they won't be the only user of that thing.[3]
- Customers need to try PostHog before they expect changes, and the handbook says it doesn't love big requirement documents from people who haven't used the product before.[4]

A YC founder can't simply claim a desk at Hogpatch: it's invite-only and not open to the whole batch, and PostHog handpicks a few YC companies to join when space opens up.[1] There is a waitlist, but you can't apply, since founders are handpicked when there's room.[2]

Once invited:
- Judy, the office manager, sends you and your cofounders a digital wallet pass that gives 24/7 self-service access, with no check-in or reservations needed.[3]
- There is no booking system for desks and phone booths; you just grab a spot when you arrive.[4]
- Each invite lasts 3 months, and if you join later you're still welcome to keep using Hogpatch after your batch ends.[5]
rows.note: Invite-only, handpicked, waitlist with no applying, 3-month invites (p944), wallet pass from Judy (p945); all accurate.

rows.answer:
A routine mutation run on Feb 19 to materialize an index triggered a bug in ClickHouse's zero-copy replication, which caused one replica to erroneously believe all of the data parts in the database were no longer referenced.[1]

- The replicas then spent roughly 11:02–19:40 deleting all of the data stored in S3 for the entire database.[2]
- Data is only moved to S3 after 24 hours and most queries are for recent data, so the volume of query errors was low and no automated alarms triggered.[2]
- There was no specific monitoring for the integrity of "cold" data in S3, and the deletion happened silently in the background without application-level errors, so dashboards stayed "green" until a node restart forced a consistency check.[3]
- At 19:40 a node crashed and failed to restart because of the large volume of missing data, and engineers found that most S3-backed data was missing.[4]

The result was loss of data collected more than 3 days ago in the US region, affecting only the Logs product.[5] Kafka's 3 days of retention saved recent activity from total loss.[6]
rows.note: ClickHouse zero-copy replication bug, triggered by the mutation, deleted the S3 data across the database (p137-138); timeline and detection details match.

rows.answer:
The handbook indicates that only recent Logs data was restored, and the older data was not. The incident caused the loss of Logs data collected more than 3 days ago in the US region.[1] Engineers determined the data was most likely unrecoverable, and disaster recovery procedures started.[2]

- The team decided to cut over to a new table and restore data from Kafka, which had 3 days of retention.[3]
- The backfill from Kafka history began on Feb 20 at 10:05 and completed at 12:21.[4]
- The 3-day Kafka retention saved PostHog from total data loss for recent activity.[5]

The handbook says one good place to start is checking whether the customer has a reverse proxy set up[1], and it gives these ways to do it:

- If the customer uses session replay, go to the replay video, select Activity > Inspector > Doctor, and search for "config". Find PostHog Config, expand api_host, and see whether the URL is one of PostHog's domains (us.i.posthog.com or eu.i.posthog.com) or one of the customer's own.[2]
- If the customer isn't using session replay, add ?__posthog_debug=true to a URL where PostHog is being called, open the console logs, type posthog.config, and look for the api_host property.[3]
- If neither method works because the customer isn't using session replay and the hosted site isn't publicly accessible, you can ask the customer on the discovery call.[4]

How to read the result: if api_host shows us.i.posthog or eu.i.posthog, they are not using a reverse proxy.[5] With either PostHog's managed reverse proxy or a non-managed one, events should populate the "Library custom API host" property. Host mapping and domains can potentially be seen in Metabase, and you should verify the setup with the customer.[6]
rows.note: An api_host of us.i/eu.i.posthog means no reverse proxy (p1060); the replay Doctor and debug-URL methods match p209-210, and the Library custom API host detail matches p223.

To propose a company-wide tool, first try it in a low-risk context[1], then open a pull request and issue, and after a decision is made, handle the vendor terms and legal review.

- Try the tool where it is easily replaced and doesn't involve sensitive data; if you're unsure what information can be shared, check with #legal first.[2]
- Open a pull request in Company Internal and, at the same time, an issue describing why the company should adopt the tool. Think about the impact on the whole company, not just your team or use case.[3]
- Once a decision to adopt is made, the person proposing the tool coordinates the next steps.[4]
- You negotiate business terms with the vendor, such as cost, number of licenses or usage limits, contract length, and implementation or onboarding details.[5]
- As soon as it looks like you'll move forward, post in #legal[6] to say a decision has been made, business terms are being negotiated, and contract documents will be shared shortly.[7]
- When documents are available, send them to #legal in an editable format such as .docx.[8]
- Legal review usually takes a few business days, and negotiations may take longer.[9] If the vendor qualifies as a subprocessor, the review is usually more involved.[10]
- The tool can be used in production once legal review is complete, contracts are signed, and any required subprocessor notice period has passed.[11]

This process doesn't apply to "cheap decisions" that are easily completed or reversed, or only affect your own work; those follow the software section of the spending money page.[12]

Yes, the handbook gives exit criteria for each opportunity stage. Bolded exit criteria are the minimum standard to advance stages, typically for smaller, more transactional deals, and a spreadsheet has more detail on each stage.[1] For the New and Existing Business record types, the criteria are:

- Problem Agreement: identified and implicated pain with specific, quantifiable metrics, a documented answer to "What happens if you do nothing?", and the buyer explicitly saying "This is a problem we need to solve".[2]
- Solution Agreement: active product usage or a completed POC/trial, a clear documentable decision for PostHog, the Economic Buyer identified (name and title), and a Champion identified (name).[3]
- Priority Agreement: budget confirmed, decision process mapped, the Economic Buyer's exact quote that this is a priority, a tested Champion, and a known compelling event.[4]
- Commercial Agreement: price agreed in writing, all commercial terms agreed, and the paper process mapped.[5]
- Vendor Approval: contract signed.[6]

The handbook's Wildfire Systems case study says the fix is to give the extension a persistent identity and cut down on identify() and /flags calls. The steps are:

- Persist the ID manually by using chrome.storage.local to store a UUID.[1] Wildfire generated this ID once and reused it across all extension contexts.[2]
- Bootstrap the identity by passing the UUID during posthog.init() with bootstrap.distinctID.[3]
- Only call identify() if the ID has changed.[4] Wildfire checked whether the existing distinct_id matched the UUID before calling identify().[5]
- Reduce /flags usage by using bootstrap.featureFlags and disabling polling if needed.[6]
- Monitor proactively with the "My PostHog Billable Usage" dashboard.[7] It showed real-time data that let Wildfire verify the fixes worked.[8]

The cause is that each new extension runtime context re-initialized PostHog without access to prior storage.[9] Local storage is isolated per context, so the SDK couldn't persist the ID and created a new anonymous ID on each wake cycle.[10] That made identify() get called repeatedly, and every identify() call refreshed feature flags.[11]

Raising the billing limit mid-cycle won't help right away: it did not retroactively unlock flags, and only new requests after the monthly reset were allowed.[12]

Also, customers should be aware early that extensions require manual handling.[13]

rows.answer:
No, not strictly. Everyone shares some work, but SMEs also own specific product groups.

- All technical support engineers, regardless of SME ownership, work on Analytics products (shared because they make up the highest proportion of tickets) and on unclassified tickets, which should be updated with the correct product group where possible.[1]
- Beyond that, SMEs own specific product groups, with one person from EU and one from NA per group to maintain timezone coverage.[2] The groups listed are Flags, Data, Replay, Observability + AI & client libraries, and Analytics.[3][4][5][6][7]
- SMEs start the day with their SME views, then move to the Technical support shared view, which has all tickets the technical support team is responsible for, once they're on top of their SME queue.[8]
- SMEs aren't locked into only their products: if caught up and the shared queue needs attention, they dive in, and if swamped they can ask for help with their SME queue.[9]
- New support engineers usually spend their first few weeks focused just on product and web analytics tickets, until they've built more familiarity with the platform.[10]

When picking tickets from a queue:
- Avoid cherry-picking and pick the ticket closest to breaching response targets.[11]
- Check whether someone else is already viewing a ticket, and communicate when in doubt.[12]
- Support team folks who work on tickets from multiple queues often assign tickets to themselves, and assign them back to the team/group when escalating.[13]

The handbook's cutoff is about $20k in annual spend: when qualifying, you consider company size, revenue and funding to judge whether they'll pay >$20k for PostHog[1], and one of the discovery qualifiers is a path to $2k/mo or $20k/year in spend[2]. A lead with no path to $20k+ annual spend is a disqualifier, and the handbook points to its section on leads below the sales assist threshold (less than $20k ARR)[3].

Beyond that dollar figure, the handbook gives these considerations for marking a lead self-serve:
- If their usage volume is around 5 million monthly events and 100,000 recordings, they should be hands-on.[4]
- If they want an annual commitment, keep them in the hands-on pipeline.[5]
- If they need help with a guided evaluation and their potential value is high enough, create a Slack Connect channel and keep them in the hands-on pipeline.[5]
- If none of these apply, move them to self-serve.[6]

For product-led leads, the handbook says it's on you to decide how you qualify, and if you think they have potential to pay more than $20k a year, you should reach out to introduce yourself and offer help.[7]
rows.note: About $20k/year potential spend (p619, p592-593, p622); the self-serve considerations match p554 and the product-led guidance matches p647.

No. The handbook says PostHog doesn't contract deliverables, and especially doesn't contract to provide deliverables by a certain date, because on principle a single customer would then be forcing PostHog to build something.[1]

- If PostHog has to walk away from a deal because it would have to compromise on these principles, it will.[2]

- Customers need to try PostHog before they expect changes. Feedback is welcome, but big requirement documents from people who haven't used the product are not.[4]

A routine mutation run on Feb 19 to materialize an index triggered a bug in ClickHouse's zero-copy replication, which caused one of the replicas to erroneously believe all of the data parts in the database were no longer referenced.[1]

- From 11:02 to 19:40 UTC, the replicas deleted all of the data stored in S3 for the entire database.[2]
- Data is only moved to S3 after 24 hours, and most queries are for recent data, so no automated alarms triggered because the volume of query errors was relatively low.[2]
- PostHog lacked specific monitoring for the integrity of "cold" data stored in S3, and the deletion happened silently in the background without application-level errors, so dashboards stayed "green" until a node restart forced a consistency check.[3]
- At 19:40 a node crashed and restarted but failed to start up because of the large volume of missing data, and engineers then discovered that the vast majority of S3-backed data was missing.[4]
- The result was the loss of data collected more than 3 days ago in the US region, affecting only the Logs product.[5]
- Kafka's 3 days of retention prevented total data loss for recent activity.[6]
rows.note: A bug in ClickHouse zero-copy replication caused the replicas to delete the S3-stored data; matches p137-138.

rows.answer:
The handbook says only part of the lost data came back. The February 19 incident caused the loss of Logs data collected more than 3 days ago in the US region.[1] By 21:45 it was determined that the data was most likely unrecoverable, and disaster recovery procedures started.[2]

- Recovery came from Kafka. The decision was made to cut over to a new table and restore data from Kafka, which has 3 days of retention.[3]
- The backfill from Kafka history began on Feb 20 at 10:05 and completed at 12:21.[4]
- The 3-day Kafka retention saved PostHog from total data loss for recent activity.[5]

So the Kafka restore covered roughly the last 3 days of data. The handbook describes the older data as lost, since it was beyond Kafka's retention.

The question could mean two things: product intents, or interest sign-ups through the coming soon menu. The handbook covers both.

- You should start tracking product intents as soon as your product is in any sort of public beta.[1] Collecting product intents should be a precursor to any sort of public release.[2]
- The reason is to start collecting data for later, when you want to determine a good activation metric, not to hyper-focus on activation numbers at this stage.[1]
- For gauging interest through sign-ups, adding items to the coming soon menu early lets you gauge interest in a new feature via sign-ups and ensures that betas have sample users ready from the moment they launch.[3] A coming soon feature should be something you expect to work on in the next 3-6 months.[4]
- Users who registered interest during the Concept stage can opt in once you move the item to beta (or alpha), which triggers an automatic notification to all subscribed users.[5]

Query PostHog's data warehouse to pull Salesforce data and create a CSV of all PostHog organization IDs for accounts you own.[1]

The handbook gives this SQL query for it:

SELECT DISTINCT posthog_org_id_c, NULL as empty_column FROM salesforce.account WHERE owner_id = 'your_salesforce_id'[2]

- To find your Salesforce ID, go to your profile and copy the text in the website URL after "/User/".[2]

Checking the customer's reverse proxy setup is a good place to start[1], and the handbook gives a few ways to do it:

- If the customer uses session replay, open a replay video, select Activity > Inspector > Doctor, search for "config", find PostHog Config, and expand api_host. Check whether the URL is one of PostHog's domains (us.i.posthog.com or eu.i.posthog.com) or one of their own.[2]
- If they aren't using session replay, add ?__posthog_debug=true to a URL where PostHog is being called, open the console logs, type posthog.config, and look for the api_host property.[3]
- If neither method is available because they don't use session replay and the hosted site isn't publicly accessible, you can ask the customer on the discovery call.[4]

If api_host shows us.i.posthog or eu.i.posthog, they are not using a reverse proxy.[5] You can also look at events: with either PostHog's managed reverse proxy or a non-managed one, events should populate the "Library custom API host" property, and you should verify the setup with the customer.[6]
rows.note: Check api_host via replay Doctor or the debug param; us/eu.i.posthog.com means no proxy. Matches p209-210, p1060 and p223.

To propose a new company-wide tool, you first try it in a low-risk context, then open a pull request in Company Internal and, at the same time, an issue describing why PostHog should adopt it.[1][2]

- Try it where it is easily replaced and doesn't involve sensitive data; if you're unsure what information can be shared, check with #legal first.[3]
- The trial is meant to check that the tool works as well as you expect, understand the consequences of introducing it, learn what data it may have access to, and let others see it in action.[4]
- Think about the impact on the whole company, not just your team or use case.[5]
- The review is a holistic weighing of risks against benefits, and the guidelines aren't a rigid checklist.[6] Many proposals won't make it past this stage, which the handbook says is good.[7]

After a decision to adopt:
- The person proposing the tool coordinates the next steps.[8]
- You negotiate business terms with the vendor, such as cost, number of licenses or usage limits, contract length, and implementation or onboarding details.[9]
- Once terms are mostly settled, the vendor's documents go through legal review before anything is signed.[10]
- As soon as it looks like you'll move forward, post in #legal to say a decision has been made, business terms are being negotiated, and contract documents will be shared shortly.[11]
- The tool can be used in production only once legal review is complete, contracts are signed, and any required subprocessor notice period has passed.[12]

If the vendor is a new subprocessor, customers must receive 14 days' notice after the agreement is finalized before it can be used in production.[13] If you're unsure whether a tool qualifies as a subprocessor, check with #legal early.[14]

This process doesn't apply to "cheap decisions" that are easily completed or reversed, or only affect your own work; those follow the software section of the spending money page.[15]
gaps: who makes the final decision on adopting a new company-wide tool
rows.note: Trial low-risk, then a PR plus an issue in Company Internal, then the proposer coordinates terms and #legal review; matches p31-34. The 'who decides' gap is accurate, since the page doesn't name a decider.

Great care should be taken when writing or modifying a GitHub Actions workflow, since Actions can access (and exfiltrate) secrets scoped to the repo, and workflows are scanned with Semgrep and CodeQL for common misconfigurations.[1]

What the handbook does say about review in general:
- Almost all PRs made to PostHog repositories need a review from another engineer.[2]
- You can request a review from someone relevant.[3]
- If you need help setting up a new GitHub App for an Action, send a message in #team-security.[4]

The Shai-Hulud write-up shows why such changes deserve scrutiny: a workflow was modified to check out the PR head commit, so code run in a trusted CI run was controlled by the PR author, which made it possible to steal the bot token.[5]

Yes. The handbook gives exit criteria for each Salesforce opportunity stage, and these are what an opportunity must meet to advance. Bolded exit criteria indicate the minimum standard for the opportunity to advance stages (for typically smaller, more transactional deals), and the spreadsheet it links has more detail on each stage's exit criteria.[1]

Stages and exit criteria for the New and Existing Business record types:

- Problem Agreement: Identified and implicated pain with specific, quantifiable metrics (time/money/risk), and the answer to "What happens if you do nothing?" documented with a real consequence.[2] The buyer explicitly said "This is a problem we need to solve" (not just "interesting").[3]
- Solution Agreement: Active product usage OR a completed POC/trial.[4] A clear, documentable decision made for PostHog (with or without comparing alternatives).[5] Economic Buyer identified (name + title).[6] Champion identified (name).[7]
- Priority Agreement: Budget confirmed (amount range OR "yes, funded").[8] Decision process mapped (who approves, what steps, timeline).[9] Economic Buyer said this is a priority (exact quote documented).[10] Champion tested (evidence they're advocating internally).[11] Compelling event known (deadline: budget cycle, launch, renewal, etc.).[12]
- Commercial Agreement: Price agreed in writing (email/quote with amount + terms).[13] All commercial terms agreed (payment terms, contract length, prepaid amount), and the paper process mapped (legal, security, procurement steps + owners + timeline).[14]
- Vendor Approval: Contract signed.[15]

Closed Won means they have signed the contract and are officially a PostHog customer.[16]

If you meant moving upward to leadership in an expansion account, that is a separate topic.

rows.answer:
The handbook recommends that extension developers persist their ID manually, bootstrap identity, avoid repeated identify() calls, reduce /flags usage, and monitor proactively.[1] The steps are:

- Persist the ID manually by using chrome.storage.local to store a UUID, which is generated once and reused across all extension contexts.[2][3]
- Bootstrap identity by passing the UUID during posthog.init() with bootstrap.distinctID.[4][5]
- Only call identify() if the ID has changed, by checking whether the existing distinct_id matches the UUID first.[6][7]
- Reduce /flags usage by using bootstrap.featureFlags and disabling polling if needed, which cuts the need for real-time flag fetches.[8][9]
- Monitor with the "My PostHog Billable Usage" dashboard, which showed real-time data to verify the fixes worked in the Wildfire case.[10][11]

The reason this happens is that each new extension runtime context re-initializes PostHog without access to prior storage, so a new anonymous ID is created on each wake cycle.[12] That triggers identify() every time, and each identify() call refreshes feature flags.[13]

Raising the billing limit mid-cycle did not retroactively unlock flags; only new requests after the monthly reset were allowed.[14]

Not exactly: everyone shares some work, but SMEs own specific product groups.

- All technical support engineers, regardless of SME ownership, work on Analytics products (shared because it represents the highest proportion of tickets) and on unclassified tickets, which should be updated with the correct product group where possible.[1]
- Beyond that, SMEs own specific product groups, with one person from EU and one from NA selected for each group to maintain timezone coverage.[2] The groups listed are Flags, Data, Replay, Observability + AI & client libraries, and Analytics.[3][4][5][6][7]
- SMEs start the day with their SME views, and once they're on top of that queue, they move to the Technical support shared view, which has all tickets the technical support team is responsible for.[8]
- They aren't locked into only their SME products: the goal is expertise, not silos, so if they're caught up they can help with the shared queue, and if they're swamped they can ask someone else to help with their SME queue.[9]
- New support engineers usually spend their first few weeks focused just on product and web analytics tickets, until they've built more familiarity with the platform as a whole.[10]

When picking tickets, the handbook says to avoid cherry-picking and to pick the ticket closest to breaching response targets.[11]

The handbook gives no single cutoff. It leaves the call to the rep, who weighs a few factors when deciding whether a lead stays hands-on or goes self-serve.

- If you feel a customer doesn't fit a hands-on flow, you mark the lead or opportunity as self serve.[1]
- If their usage volume is around 5 million monthly events and 100,000 recordings, they should be hands-on.[2]
- If they want an annual commitment, keep them in the hands-on pipeline.[3]
- If they need help with a guided evaluation and their potential value is high enough, create a Slack Connect channel and keep them in the hands-on pipeline.[3]
- If none of those apply, move them to self-serve.[4]

For leads from companies already using PostHog, if you think they have potential to end up paying more than $20k a year, you should reach out to introduce yourself and offer help.[5] How you qualify the lead is up to you.[5]

For the "no interaction" option, you can use it when a lead does not meet the necessary qualifications for direct engagement and the automated self serve emails would be sufficient for successful onboarding.[6]
